items.title: Convex, strictly convex, concave, strictly concave, and midpoint-convex real functions on an interval
For a convex function and $x<y<z$, the three secant slopes satisfy $s(x,y)\le s(x,z)\le s(y,z)$
items.strategy: Rewrite each point as a convex combination of the other two and clear only positive denominators. State all three inequalities, including the middle whole-chord slope, so later one-sided-limit arguments never silently strengthen the lemma.

items.title: A convex real function is Lipschitz on every closed bounded subinterval of the interior of its domain, hence continuous throughout the interior
items.strategy: Trap all secant slopes on a compactly contained interval between two fixed outer secant slopes supplied by the three-slope lemma. Convert the resulting difference-quotient bound into a Lipschitz estimate and then continuity, keeping endpoints outside the claim unless the function is separately continuous there.

items.title: The left and right derivatives of a real function as one-sided limits of its difference quotient
A convex function on an open interval has finite left and right derivatives everywhere, with $f'_-(u)\le f'_+(u)\le (f(v)-f(u))/(v-u)\le f'_-(v)\le f'_+(v)$ for $u<v$
items.strategy: Use monotonicity and local boundedness of the appropriate secant-slope functions to obtain their one-sided limits. Pass the finite three-slope inequalities to those limits and identify the limits with the one-sided derivatives exactly as defined on the preceding item.

items.title: A convex function on an open interval is differentiable except at at most countably many points
items.strategy: Let $g=f'_+$. The ordered one-sided-derivative inequalities make $g$ nondecreasing; identify its left limit at $c$ with $f'_-(c)$. Thus a failure of differentiability is a jump discontinuity of $g$, and Froda's theorem makes the exceptional set at most countable.

items.title: A supporting line of slope $m$ for a real function at an interior point
Every slope between the left and right derivatives of a convex function gives a supporting line
items.strategy: For $x<c$, compare the secant slope from $x$ to $c$ with $f'_-(c)$; for $x>c$, compare $f'_+(c)$ with the secant slope from $c$ to $x$. Insert the chosen slope between the one-sided derivatives and rearrange, treating $x=c$ by equality.

items.title: A differentiable function on an open interval is convex if and only if its derivative is nondecreasing
items.strategy: In the forward direction specialize the ordered one-sided-derivative inequality to ordinary derivatives. In the reverse direction use derivative monotonicity and the derivative-sign theorem on either side of a base point to establish the tangent supporting-line inequality, then recover the convex-combination inequality from the two endpoint supporting inequalities.

items.title: A differentiable convex function on an open interval has a continuous derivative
items.strategy: The preceding equivalence makes the derivative nondecreasing. Darboux's theorem says every derivative has the intermediate-value property, and the published monotone-derivative corollary then gives continuity without assuming a second derivative.

items.title: A twice-differentiable function on an open interval is convex if and only if its second derivative is nonnegative
items.strategy: Apply the differentiable convexity criterion to $f$, then apply the published derivative-sign/monotonicity theorem to $f'$. Preserve both directions and the weak inequality; do not replace nonnegative by positive.

items.title: Midpoint convexity gives the convexity inequality at every dyadic weight $k/2^n$
items.strategy: Induct on $n$, with $0\le k\le 2^n$. Even numerators reduce to the preceding level; odd numerators are the midpoint of the adjacent even dyadic weights. Keep the $n=0$ level and the endpoint weights $0,1$ explicit under the library's zero-based natural-number convention.

items.title: A continuous midpoint-convex function on an interval is convex
items.strategy: For a fixed weight in $[0,1]$, use the Archimedean property to choose dyadic weights converging to it (derive the needed approximation inline because the later dyadic-topology item is unavailable at this order). Apply the dyadic inequality and pass to the limit by continuity. Cover weights $0$ and $1$ directly.

items.title: Finite Jensen inequality for a convex function and nonnegative weights summing to one
items.strategy: Induct on a positive natural number of terms. Split off the final weight. When it equals one, all earlier weights vanish; otherwise normalize the preceding weights by their positive sum, apply induction, and then apply two-point convexity. State the $n=1$ base separately so no empty normalized family is formed.

items.title: Every local minimum of a convex function on an interval is a global minimum
items.strategy: If a point with smaller value existed, convex combinations with weights tending to zero would lie arbitrarily close to the local minimizer and have smaller values. Use the local-neighbourhood radius explicitly and include the one-point-domain case.

items.title: A strictly convex function has at most one global minimizer
items.strategy: Two distinct minimizers would have a midpoint in the interval whose value is strictly below their common minimum. Treat the empty minimizer set and singleton domain as allowed, not as existence claims.

items.title: An inflection point as a point of continuity where convexity changes to concavity or conversely
A continuous function whose second derivative has opposite signs on the two sides of a point has an inflection point there
items.strategy: Use the second-derivative convexity criterion on each one-sided interval, applying it to $-f$ for the concave side, and then invoke the definition's continuity clause. Do not claim that $f''(c)=0$ alone is sufficient.

items.title: Convexity conventions, endpoint scope, dyadic approximation, and the exact use of the Axiom of Choice in the midpoint-convex counterexample
The absolute-value function is convex
items.strategy: Apply the triangle inequality to $|\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y|$ and absolute homogeneity for the nonnegative coefficients. Link in a remark, but do not cite as a dependency, the already-published companion-page counterexample showing nondifferentiability at zero.

items.title: Finite Jensen for $x\mapsto x^2$ gives that the square of a weighted mean is at most the weighted mean of the squares
items.strategy: Verify convexity of the square by expanding the Jensen gap as $\lambda(1-\lambda)(x-y)^2\ge0$, then instantiate finite Jensen. Include arbitrary finite positive length, zero weights, and the equality statement only when it is actually proved.

items.title: Assuming Choice, a Hamel coefficient map is midpoint convex but discontinuous and therefore not convex
items.strategy: Choose a Hamel basis vector and its published coefficient map. Additivity and rational homogeneity give midpoint equality. The nontrivial complementary span shows the map is not of the form $x\mapsto cx$; the published Cauchy-equation regularity theorem then makes it discontinuous. Since convex functions are continuous on the interior, it is not convex.

items.title: $x\mapsto x^3$ changes from concave to convex at zero and has an inflection point there
items.strategy: Compute the first and second derivatives from the power rule. The second derivative is negative to the left of zero and positive to the right; continuity at zero and the sign-change corollary finish. Explicitly contrast this with the already-published $x^4$ example, without depending on that B-page item.

title: The Total Derivative in R^m -> R^n

items.title: A linear map $L:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$ in Euclidean coordinates
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$
items.strategy: Expand $h$ in the published standard basis, use linearity to obtain $Lh=\sum_j h_jL(e_j)$, and read off the unique matrix columns. Bound the norm by the finite triangle inequality and $|h_j|\le\|h\|_2$, taking $K=\sum_j\|L(e_j)\|_2$. Check $m=0$ is outside the standing hypotheses and zero maps give $K=0$.

items.title: A convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ contains every line segment between two of its points
Directional derivatives and partial derivatives of a map $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$
The total (Fréchet) derivative $Df(a)$ as the linear first-order approximation with $o(\|h\|_2)$ remainder
The total derivative at a point is unique
items.strategy: If $L$ and $M$ both satisfy the remainder estimate, test along $h=tv$ inside an open ball about the point. Divide by $|t|$ for $t\ne0$ and use an epsilon contradiction to obtain $(L-M)v=0$ for every $v$, including $v=0$ separately.

items.title: Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity
items.strategy: Bound $Df(a)h$ by the Euclidean linear-map lemma and make the normalized remainder at most one on a sufficiently small ball. The triangle inequality gives $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le(K+1)\|h\|_2$, from which epsilon-delta continuity follows; keep the zero-map and zero-increment cases explicit.

items.title: The Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives and the gradient in the scalar-valued case
A total derivative computes every directional derivative, and its matrix is the Jacobian
items.strategy: Restrict the total remainder estimate to $h=tv$. After division by $t$, homogeneity makes the remainder tend to zero and the derivative of $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ equals $Df(a)v$. Specialize to standard basis vectors and invoke the matrix-column representation to identify the Jacobian, preserving the $v=0$ case.

items.title: For a differentiable scalar field, $D_vf(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$ and the unit direction of steepest ascent is the normalized gradient
items.strategy: Use the Jacobian representation in the scalar case to obtain the inner-product formula. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds unit-direction derivatives by the gradient norm, with equality in the normalized gradient direction when the gradient is nonzero; when it is zero, every directional derivative is zero and there is no unique steepest direction.

items.title: Sums and scalar multiples of totally differentiable maps are totally differentiable with the expected derivatives
items.strategy: Add or scale the two remainder identities and use the norm triangle inequality or absolute homogeneity. Verify that the proposed derivative is linear, and split the scalar-zero case only where division by its absolute value would otherwise occur.

items.title: The chain rule for total derivatives: $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$
items.strategy: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=Ah+r(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)-g(f(a))=Bk+s(k)$. The local linear bound makes $k=O(\|h\|)$, so $s(k)=o(\|k\|)=o(\|h\|)$, while boundedness of $B$ gives $B r(h)=o(\|h\|)$. Treat $k=0$ without forming the normalized outer remainder and verify the composite linear map explicitly.

items.title: Small coordinate-by-coordinate increments stay inside a Euclidean ball and telescope the total increment
items.strategy: For $h\in\mathbb{R}^m$, define $p_j=a+\sum_{k<j}h_ke_k$. The norm of each coordinate prefix is at most $\|h\|_2$, so a small increment keeps every $p_j$ in the chosen ball. The finite telescoping identity expresses $f(a+h)-f(a)$ as the sum of the increments $f(p_{j+1})-f(p_j)$.

items.title: If all partial derivatives exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous at a point, then the map is totally differentiable there with Jacobian derivative
items.strategy: Choose a ball where every partial derivative vector is uniformly close to its value at the base point. Telescope along coordinate segments using the preceding lemma; apply the published vector mean-value inequality to each segment after subtracting the fixed linear term. Sum the errors and compare the coordinate $1$-norm with the Euclidean norm. Verify the Jacobian map is linear before invoking the definition.

items.title: On a convex open set, a uniform bound $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ implies $\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2$
items.strategy: Parametrize the segment from $x$ to $y$ by $\gamma(t)=x+t(y-x)$. Convexity keeps the curve in the domain, the chain rule gives $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))(y-x)$, and the published vector mean-value inequality supplies the endpoint estimate. Treat $x=y$ directly and use no global operator-norm definition.

items.title: A totally differentiable map with zero derivative on a convex open set is constant
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative mean-value inequality with $M=0$ to arbitrary points of the domain. Include the empty-domain case (vacuously constant under the library's definition) and singleton/zero-dimensional exclusions explicitly rather than importing the later connected-open-set theorem.

items.title: Dimension, openness, norm, Jacobian, and the native Euclidean linear-map agreement seam

title: The Total Derivative in R^m -> R^n: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The polynomial map $(x,y)\mapsto(1+x+2y+x^2,\,2x+3y+xy)$ and its Jacobian
items.strategy: Compute all four partial derivatives with the one-variable algebra and power rules. Their continuity makes the continuous-partials theorem applicable, and the resulting Jacobian matrix gives the total derivative at an arbitrary point. Verify one increment expansion directly as a check on the matrix.

items.title: $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ has both partial derivatives at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: Define the value at the origin to be zero. Both coordinate-axis restrictions are identically zero, so both partial derivatives exist and vanish. Along $y=x\ne0$ the function is $1/2$, contradicting continuity at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^4+y^2)$ tends to zero on every line through the origin but not along $y=x^2$
items.strategy: Define the origin value to be zero. Substitute $(x,y)=(ta,tb)$ and separate $b=0$ from $b\ne0$ to show every straight-line restriction tends to zero. Along $(t,t^2)$ the value is $1/2$, so the map is not continuous at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ has every directional derivative at the origin but is not totally differentiable there
items.strategy: Compute the directional derivative along $v=(a,b)$ as $a^2b/(a^2+b^2)$ for $v\ne0$ and zero for $v=0$. Exhibit a failure of additivity of this direction map. If a total derivative existed, the directional-derivative theorem would make the map linear, a contradiction.

items.title: The map $y(x^2+y^2)/x$ off the line $x=0$, extended by zero on that line, has every directional derivative zero at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: On every fixed line through the origin the function is quadratic in the line parameter, so the directional difference quotient tends to zero. Along the curved path $x=y^3$ the values tend to one, proving discontinuity and hence failure of total differentiability.

items.title: A locally constant step map on the disconnected open set $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ has zero total derivative but is not globally Lipschitz
items.strategy: In the $\mathbb{R}^1$ identification, take value zero on the negative component and one on the positive component. Each point has a neighbourhood on which the map is constant, so its total derivative is zero. The points $-t$ and $t$ have image distance one and domain distance $2t$, which defeats every proposed global Lipschitz constant for small positive $t$.
